ledger.sentence: CT stands for computed tomography.
ledger.note: Title of NIBIB page: Computed Tomography (CT).

ledger.sentence: A CT scanner rotates an X-ray source around the body while the person lies on a bed that moves through a ring shaped like a doughnut.
ledger.note: NIBIB: patient lies on bed moving through donut-shaped gantry.

ledger.sentence: Detectors on the opposite side pick up the X-rays, and a computer turns each rotation into a thin cross-sectional slice.
ledger.note: NIBIB: detectors across from source; each rotation constructs 2D slice.

ledger.sentence: The slices can be stacked to make a three-dimensional image.
ledger.note: NIBIB.

ledger.sentence: The NHS lists CT scans among the tests that use X-rays to give more detailed images than a standard X-ray.
ledger.note: NHS X-ray page lists CT scans among other types giving more detailed images.

ledger.sentence: Instructions differ between hospitals, and the appointment letter has the local details.
ledger.note: Trust leaflets differ on fasting (2 h vs 4 h); letter statement is a paraphrase of that variation.

ledger.sentence: One trust asks for no food for two hours and about half a litre of water beforehand, while another asks for no solid food for four hours and says drinks are fine.
ledger.note: Search summary: two trusts' differing fasting rules. Note: contains numbers, trust-specific. Second pass to decide.

ledger.sentence: Some scans of the abdomen or pelvis need a larger amount of fluid or a drink containing contrast beforehand.
ledger.note: Summary: some abdominal/pelvic scans need up to a litre or oral contrast drink.

ledger.sentence: Some people have a blood test first, mainly to check how well the kidneys are working.
ledger.note: Summary: some scans need blood test first mainly to check kidney function.

ledger.sentence: Metal items such as zips, jewellery and clips may need to come off, and a gown may be provided.
ledger.note: Summary: metal items may need to come off; gown.

ledger.sentence: Staff ask about allergies, especially to iodine or to earlier contrast dye, and about medicines the person takes.
ledger.note: Summary: tell staff about allergies, iodine, previous contrast reaction, medicines.

ledger.sentence: The person lies on a flat, motorised table that slides into the scanner.
ledger.note: Trust leaflets: motorised table slides into ring-shaped scanner.

ledger.sentence: They are asked to keep very still and may be asked to hold their breath for a few seconds.
ledger.note: Summary.

ledger.sentence: Sources give different lengths for the scan itself, from a few minutes to around 20 minutes, and a visit can last an hour or two.
ledger.note: Summary: 10-20 min; 5-30 min; MedlinePlus head scans minutes; visit up to 1-2 h.

ledger.sentence: MedlinePlus says the scan is painless but can be uncomfortable because the person has to stay still.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus.

ledger.sentence: Most people can go home or return to normal activities straight away.
ledger.note: Trust summary.

ledger.sentence: Contrast is a substance that makes blood vessels, organs or other tissues easier to see.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus/NIBIB.

ledger.sentence: Depending on the area, it may be given by mouth, through a vein, or by enema.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus: oral, IV or enema.

ledger.sentence: The type given through a vein usually contains iodine, and trust leaflets state that it is not radioactive.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus: iodine; trust leaflet: not radioactive.

ledger.sentence: It goes in through a small tube, called a cannula, in the arm or hand.
ledger.note: Summary.

ledger.sentence: It can cause a warm flush, a metallic taste or a feeling of needing to pass urine, and these usually pass quickly.
ledger.note: Summary and MedlinePlus: warm, flushed feeling, metallic taste.

ledger.sentence: Serious allergic reactions are rare, and milder reactions such as a rash, itching or nausea are possible.
ledger.note: Summary and MedlinePlus.

ledger.sentence: Rarely the dye leaks into the tissue around the vein and causes swelling or discomfort.
ledger.note: Summary.

ledger.sentence: Effects on the kidneys are uncommon and occur mainly in people who already have kidney problems, so staff check kidney function and sometimes suggest extra fluids.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus: kidney strain, providers check kidney function; Lancs: staff may suggest fluids.

ledger.sentence: Some trusts ask people to wait for a short time after an injection so staff can check for a delayed reaction.
ledger.note: Summary: wait 15-30 minutes. Number omitted.

ledger.sentence: Difficulty breathing or swelling of the face after an injection is an emergency, and a 999 call is the route.
ledger.note: Textbook signposting.

ledger.sentence: CT uses ionising radiation, and the dose is higher than for a standard X-ray, although staff keep it as low as possible.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus/NIBIB.

ledger.sentence: MedlinePlus says having many X-rays or CT scans over time may raise the risk of cancer, but the risk from any one scan is small.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus.

ledger.sentence: Children are more sensitive to radiation, and scanner settings for children are adjusted to lower the dose.
ledger.note: NIBIB summary.

ledger.sentence: Trust leaflets say people who might be pregnant should check with the department before the scan.
ledger.note: Summary: pregnant patients advised to check with the department first.

ledger.sentence: The NHS describes X-ray tests as safe, with a very small cancer risk linked to having many of them.
ledger.note: NHS X-ray page.

ledger.sentence: GOV.UK safety advice describes the risks from properly justified imaging as far smaller than the risks of the conditions being investigated, and the added chance of cancer as very small and appearing years or decades later.
ledger.note: GOV.UK summary (7-4, 7-5).

ledger.sentence: It lists CT among the examinations that carry a low risk even though they involve more images or higher doses.
ledger.note: GOV.UK summary (7-6).

ledger.sentence: Trust leaflets add that the benefit of a scan usually outweighs the small risk.
ledger.note: Summary: benefit usually outweighs risk.

ledger.sentence: A radiologist reviews the images and sends a report to the doctor who asked for the scan.
ledger.note: Trust leaflets and MedlinePlus.

ledger.sentence: That doctor then discusses the results with the person.
ledger.note: Leeds: results discussed with referring doctor.

ledger.sentence: Timing varies by hospital, and leaflets quote from about one or two weeks to about four weeks.
ledger.note: Summary: two weeks to four weeks; NHS page 1-2 weeks.

ledger.sentence: Results are not given on the day.
ledger.note: Summary: won't get results on the day.

ledger.sentence: A CT scanner rotates an X-ray source around the body, and a computer builds cross-sectional slices that can be stacked into a three-dimensional picture.
ledger.note: NIBIB: rotating x-ray source, detectors, computer slices, 3D.

ledger.sentence: CT uses more radiation than a standard X-ray, the amount is kept as low as possible, and the risk from a single scan is small.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus/NIBIB: higher than a standard x-ray, kept low; risk from any one scan small.

ledger.sentence: Some scans use an injected iodine-based dye called contrast, which can cause a warm flush and a metallic taste that usually pass quickly.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus: common IV contrast contains iodine; warm flush, metallic taste; Lancs leaflet.

ledger.sentence: A radiologist reviews the images and sends a report to the doctor who requested the scan, who then discusses it with the person.
ledger.note: Trust leaflets: radiologist report to requesting doctor.

ledger.sentence: A CT scan uses X-rays and a computer to build slice pictures of the body. This guide covers preparation, contrast dye, radiation and when results arrive.
ledger.note: Summary restates the supported sentences below.
